snip.t: *Exam‑style tip:* Remember that portal hypertension is the hallmark of variceal bleeding; pain and NSAID history point to ulcer; retching points to Mallory‑Weiss; massive, rapid bleeding with shock is typical of varices.
Esophageal variceal bleeding should also be suspected with such a history, because hepatic cirrhosis is likely to be present.

Clinical Relevance: Synthetic somatostatin analogs (e.g., octreotide, lanreotide) are used therapeutically to treat conditions involving excessive hormone secretion, such as acromegaly (excess GH), neuroendocrine tumors, and variceal bleeding.

qs.q: A patient with suspected variceal bleeding is scheduled for an urgent diagnostic and therapeutic procedure. Within what timeframe should this endoscopy be performed?
qs.e: Endoscopy for suspected variceal bleeding should be performed within 12 hours, whereas general upper GI bleeding endoscopy is performed within 24 hours. Prompt intervention is critical due to the high mortality of variceal bleeding.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

qs.q: A patient with refractory variceal bleeding has a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube inserted as a temporary bridge. What is the maximum recommended duration this tube should remain in place?
qs.e: Balloon tamponade is a temporary life-saving measure that should not be left in place for more than 24 to 48 hours to avoid complications like oesophageal necrosis and rupture. Leaving it for 5 days significantly increases the risk of tissue ischaemia.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

qs.q: A 48-year-old cirrhotic patient with variceal bleeding receives antibiotic prophylaxis upon admission. Which of the following is an accepted regimen that reduces infection and mortality?
qs.e: Ceftriaxone or ciprofloxacin is recommended for antibiotic prophylaxis in variceal bleeding to reduce infection and mortality. Vancomycin and metronidazole do not cover the typical gram-negative organisms seen in spontaneous bacterial peritonitis prophylaxis.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

qs.q: A patient requires a rescue procedure for uncontrolled variceal bleeding that fails medical and endoscopic treatment. Which intervention successfully reduces the portal pressure gradient to below 12 mmHg?
o: Endoscopic balloon dilation of the portal vein
qs.e: TIPS (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt) is a rescue treatment for uncontrolled bleeding that reduces the portal pressure gradient below 12 mmHg. Diagnostic catheterisation does not alter portal pressure.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

qs.q: During the resuscitation of a patient with variceal bleeding, fluid and blood product administration must be carefully controlled. What is the target haemoglobin level during active resuscitation to avoid worsening portal hypertension?
qs.e: Resuscitation in variceal bleeding should be cautious and avoid over-transfusion, targeting a restrictive haemoglobin of 7 to 8 g/dL. Over-transfusion increases portal pressure and worsens bleeding.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

qs.q: When administering vasopressin for variceal bleeding, why must nitroglycerin be co-administered?
o: To protect the coronary arteries from vasopressin-induced vasoconstriction
To enhance the splanchnic vasoconstrictive potency of the administered drug
To counteract systemic hypotension caused by the primary medication
To prevent reflex tachycardia and immediate hepatic encephalopathy
qs.e: Vasopressin is a potent systemic and splanchnic vasoconstrictor that can cause coronary ischaemia, so nitroglycerin is given concurrently to protect the coronary arteries. Terlipressin is an alternative that does not routinely require nitroglycerin.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

qs.q: A 45-year-old man presents with acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding due to oesophageal varices. What is considered the endoscopic treatment of choice for acute variceal bleeding?
qs.e: Endoscopic variceal band ligation is the treatment of choice for variceal bleeding, while sclerotherapy and cyanoacrylate glue are alternative options. Adrenaline injection is typically combined with other modalities for peptic ulcer bleeding.
qs.s: Gastrointestinal Endoscopy: Upper GI Endoscopy, Colonoscopy,: MCQs

qs.q: Which of the following conditions is notably a major etiology for variceal bleeding specifically in Egypt due to a high regional prevalence?
qs.e: Variceal bleeding is common in Egyptians due to the high prevalence of hepatitis C and Schistosomiasis. Helicobacter pylori is classically associated with peptic ulcer disease rather than variceal bleeding.

ai.title: Variceal Bleeding
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Acute upper GI hemorrhage from esophageal or gastric varices due to portal hypertension. Recognise severity, identify precipitating liver disease, and act quickly with resuscitation, vasoactive drugs and endoscopic control.

sections.p: Bleeding from dilated portosystemic collaterals at the gastro‑oesophageal junction in the setting of portal hypertension.
b: Portal hypertension defined by hepatic venous pressure gradient (HVPG) >12 mmHg
Endoscopy shows varices with red wale signs or active spurting

sections.p: Use the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) grading: Grade I (small, no red signs), Grade II (medium, red signs), Grade III (large, red signs or active bleed).
b: Shock (SBP <90 mmHg, HR >100) = high‑risk
MELD ≥15 predicts poor outcome

sections.p: Portal hypertension from chronic liver disease is the dominant cause; in low‑resource settings add infections that accelerate decompensation.
b: Alcoholic cirrhosis
Viral hepatitis B/C
Schistosomiasis‑related peri‑portal fibrosis
HIV‑associated liver disease
TB or malaria‑related sepsis precipitating decompensation

sections.p: Sudden haematemesis (often massive) with or without melena, signs of chronic liver disease and possible shock.
b: Coffee‑ground vomit if slower bleed
History of retching suggests Mallory‑Weiss, not varices
NSAID use points to ulcer

t.b: Assess hemodynamic stability; hypotension or tachycardia indicates need for urgent resuscitation
Hemoglobin drop quantifies blood loss; a fall >2 g/dL is significant
Detect coagulopathy common in cirrhosis; correct if INR >1.5 before endoscopy
Calculate MELD; high scores guide prognosis and transplant referral
Confirms variceal source, grades varices, allows therapeutic banding
Shows portal vein diameter, splenomegaly, ascites – indirect evidence of portal hypertension

sections.p: Uncontrolled hemorrhage leads to hypovolemic shock, aspiration, and multi‑organ failure.
b: Persistent bleeding >2 h despite therapy
Re‑bleed within 5 days
Development of hepatic encephalopathy or hepatorenal syndrome

sections.p: Stabilise, reduce portal pressure, achieve endoscopic control, then prevent recurrence.
b: IV crystalloids + blood transfusion targeting Hb 7‑8 g/dL
Urgent endoscopic band ligation (EBL) of bleeding varices
If endoscopic control fails, insert Sengstaken–Blakemore tube as bridge to radiologic or surgical therapy
Avoid non‑selective NSAIDs and avoid routine proton‑pump inhibitors unless ulcer suspected

sections.p: After haemostasis, reduce portal pressure long‑term and monitor for re‑bleed.
b: Non‑selective beta‑blocker (e.g., propranolol) titrated to HR 55‑60 bpm, if tolerated
Repeat endoscopy in 2‑4 weeks to confirm eradication
Vaccinate against hepatitis B, HAV; screen for HCV and treat
Counselling on alcohol abstinence and safe herbal medicine use
Peptic ulcer bleed – usually associated with NSAID use, epigastric pain, and ulcer crater on endoscopy
Mallory‑Weiss tear – history of forceful retching, linear mucosal laceration, no portal hypertension
Gastric antral vascular ectasia (GAVE) – “water‑melon stomach” appearance, chronic slow bleed
Normal INR does not exclude coagulopathy in cirrhosis; consider viscoelastic testing if available
Hemoglobin may appear stable if patient received fluids; always compare to baseline

whenToSeekHelp: Signs of hepatic encephalopathy or renal failure

faq.q: Why give antibiotics in variceal bleed?
faq.a: Infection precipitates re‑bleeding; prophylactic ceftriaxone reduces mortality.

faq.q: When is a Sengstaken tube indicated?
faq.a: When endoscopic therapy fails or is unavailable and bleeding remains uncontrolled.

faq.q: Can beta‑blockers be started during an acute bleed?
faq.a: No; start after haemostasis once the patient is euvolemic.

exam: What are the first three steps in managing a patient with suspected variceal bleed? — Assess airway, start IV fluids and blood, give terlipressin and antibiotics before endoscopy.
How does the presence of red wale signs change your management? — Indicates high‑risk varices; urgent endoscopic banding is mandatory.

A patient with cirrhosis presents with haematemesis and a normal INR. What does this mean for your plan? — Coagulation may still be impaired; correct with fresh frozen plasma if invasive procedure is needed.
Why is a non‑selective beta‑blocker contraindicated in acute variceal bleeding? — It can worsen hypotension and reduce perfusion before haemostasis is achieved.
Differentiate variceal bleed from Mallory‑Weiss tear on history and endoscopy. — Mallory‑Weiss follows retching, shows linear mucosal laceration; varices are dilated veins with red signs.

What is the role of the Sengstaken–Blakemore tube and its limitations? — Provides temporary tamponade when endoscopic control fails; risks include aspiration and esophageal necrosis, so it is a bridge only.
Explain how portal hypertension leads to variceal formation. — Elevated HVPG >12 mmHg forces blood through collateral channels at the gastro‑oesophageal junction, dilating submucosal veins.
In a low‑resource setting without endoscopy, what is the best alternative to confirm variceal bleed? — Doppler ultrasound showing portal hypertension plus clinical signs of chronic liver disease.
